opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think we need to be quite careful with that word, "maturity." If by maturity we mean a general-purpose humanoid robot that can walk into any home, any factory, and just handle whatever task you throw at it, the way a person would, then no, I don't think that happens in one or two years. I'd be misleading people if I said otherwise.

But I also don't think the picture is pessimistic. What I expect in the next one to two years is that we'll see embodied intelligence become genuinely useful in specific, well-defined scenarios. Think retail, pharmacies, warehouse picking, some kinds of factory material handling, places where the environment is semi-structured, the set of objects is large but bounded, and the value of automating it is clear. In those settings I think robots will move from demos to real deployment, running for long hours and earning their keep commercially.

The core bottleneck, in my view, is still data. Language models had the whole internet to learn from. For robots, there's no equivalent ocean of action data. Teleoperation data is expensive and slow to collect, and it doesn't scale the way we need. That's why my group and I have put a lot of emphasis on synthetic data and simulation: generating large amounts of physically plausible training data, pretraining on that, and then using a relatively small amount of real-world data to close the gap. I believe that path is how we get generalization at a reasonable cost.

The other thing people underestimate is the gap between "works in a video" and "works ten thousand times in a row." A 90% success rate looks great on social media, but in a store, a 10% failure rate means somebody has to come clean up after the robot constantly. Getting from 90 to 99 to 99.9 is where the real engineering effort goes, and that's not something you leapfrog in a year.

So my overall assessment is this: one to two years is a window for embodied intelligence to prove its commercial value in vertical scenarios and to build the data flywheel. The truly general-purpose moment, the "ChatGPT moment" for robots that everyone talks about, I think is further out, maybe three to five years or more, and it will come from accumulating capabilities across many of these real deployments rather than one sudden breakthrough.

r001.rationale: The response discusses data and reliability bottlenecks, but does not say that understanding human-like central motor control remains primitive.

r002.rationale: It places the general-purpose moment three to five years or more away, but does not characterize embodied intelligence as having decades of exploration ahead.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says a general-purpose humanoid robot will not reach maturity within one or two years.

fable-5.1.text:
I think "one or two years to maturity" is too optimistic, and I'd push back on it a bit, even though I'm someone who has bet my career on this field.

Let me separate two things. There is the maturity of the *technology*, and there is the maturity of the *industry*. People tend to conflate them.

On the technology side, we have made genuine progress, and the pace is real. Large models have solved a problem that robotics struggled with for decades, which is understanding the world and understanding what a human actually wants. Perception and language are no longer the bottleneck. But the hard part of embodied intelligence was never understanding, it was acting. Manipulation in an open environment, with deformable objects, with contact, with friction, with uncertainty about what is in a drawer before you open it. The data for that does not exist on the internet. You cannot scrape a trillion tokens of "how a hand feels when it grasps a wet cup." So we are building that data from scratch, through teleoperation, through simulation, through synthetic data, and every one of those routes has a cost and a sim-to-real gap we are still closing.

My honest view is that in one or two years we will see very impressive demos and a few narrow deployments that actually make money. Logistics, structured factory tasks, maybe some commercial settings where the environment is controlled. What we will not see is a general-purpose robot that you can put into an arbitrary home and have it do an arbitrary chore reliably. "Reliably" is the key word. A demo that works ninety percent of the time is exciting. A product that fails ten percent of the time is unusable, and in a home, possibly dangerous.

I'd also say the industry maturity question is almost more important. Right now capital is flowing in fast, valuations are high, and there is a sense that whoever has the most impressive video wins. That is a bubble dynamic, and bubbles are not necessarily bad, the internet bubble built a lot of real infrastructure. But many of the current teams will not survive, and the ones that do will be the ones that found a real task with a real customer and ground through the boring engineering of reliability.

So if you ask me for a timeline: one to two years for the first commercially meaningful narrow applications, roughly five years for robots that are broadly useful in semi-structured environments, and I would not put a confident number on true general-purpose household robots. I'd rather be the person who said "slower than you think" and was wrong, than the person who promised the moon and burned the trust of the whole field.

r001.rationale: It says robots still struggle with acting and manipulation, but does not characterize understanding of human-like central motor control as primitive.

r002.rationale: It gives timelines of roughly five years for broad usefulness and no confident timeline for general-purpose household robots, but does not say decades of further exploration lie ahead.

r003.rationale: It calls maturity in one or two years too optimistic and says that period will bring narrow applications, not general-purpose robots.

astra-6.text:
I think one or two years is enough to see significant progress, but calling it maturity would be too optimistic. It depends on what we mean by mature. If we mean robots performing a clearly defined task in a controlled environment, then we may see useful products within that period. If we mean a robot entering an unfamiliar home and reliably handling whatever people ask of it, that is a much higher bar.

The difficulty is that a convincing demonstration and a dependable product are very different things. A robot has to cope with variations in objects, lighting, and physical surroundings, and it needs to recover when something goes wrong. Even a relatively small failure rate becomes a serious issue when it operates all day.

So I would expect the next year or two to bring more applications in narrowly defined settings. Those deployments can help us gather experience and improve the systems. But broad maturity will depend on reliability, cost, and the ability to generalize—not simply on whether we can produce an impressive demo.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reliability and generalization but does not characterize the field’s understanding of human-like central motor control as primitive.

r002.rationale: The response expects progress and narrow deployments over the next year or two, but does not say decades of further exploration lie ahead.

r003.rationale: It says calling maturity within one or two years would be too optimistic and distinguishes near-term narrow applications from broader maturity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one or two years is enough to see significant progress, but calling embodied intelligence mature would be premature. The key question is what we mean by maturity. If we mean robots performing specific tasks reliably in a controlled environment, that’s a much more achievable goal. If we mean a robot entering an unfamiliar home and handling all kinds of tasks safely, that’s a very different standard.

The difficulty is that a robot has to close the loop between perception, decision-making, and physical action. It has to deal with uncertainty, recognize failures, and recover. A convincing demonstration is one thing; doing the same task reliably every day is another.

So I’d expect useful applications to emerge gradually, starting with situations where the tasks and environments are relatively structured. I’m optimistic about progress over the next couple of years, but cautious about setting a deadline for the whole field to reach maturity.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the challenges of robot perception, decisions, and action, but says nothing about how primitive the field’s understanding of human-like central motor control is.

r002.rationale: It expects gradual progress over the next couple of years but does not characterize the field as having decades of exploration ahead.

r003.rationale: It says calling embodied intelligence mature in one or two years would be premature and is cautious about setting that deadline for the whole field.
